title: E26 - Exploring Legal Tech Investments in the Post-ChatGPT World with Chris Fisher and Jonathan Levy
author: Chris Fisher · Jonathan Levy

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source contains only podcast closing remarks and provides no substantive claim, evidence or argument about user-led legal AI adoption, capability readiness, verification, market scenarios or governance. Its position relative to the cluster therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition as an investment thesis: corporate legal teams may use AI to improve efficiency and reduce external legal spending, while law firms remain customers and users of the same or related systems. Its claims are predictive rather than evidence of realised, market-wide insourcing.
qs: And either the external person is going to use it to help smooth over some business model changes and or the corporate in house will use it to reduce some of the spend externally and be more efficient.

And so ideally, you know, you can sell to AM 200, you can sell to the law firms, but you can also sell internally because it's just going to be users using a solution because as you move from a record keeping system to a system of action, it is the act of practicing and that can be in house or it can be external and it's probably going to be shared.

kp.k: Legal AI attracts stronger entrepreneurial talent
kp.d: Levy reports that YC is seeing more talented founders entering legal technology than previously, and presents this as a reason for increased optimism rather than a measured industry finding. He clarifies that YC invests primarily in talent, qualifying Abramowitz's recollection that Sam Altman called legal a major investment focus. Fisher attributes founder interest to difficult technical problems, legal context, existing software expenditure and high human operating costs.
qs: And lately, there's been much more talent coming into legal than ever.
we invest in talent more than anything and just get really talented people.
It is a huge market that has a, and it already has software spend in it. It has essentially a high human and operating cost in it.

kp.k: Buyers have become more receptive to early-stage startups
kp.d: Levy contrasts earlier committee barriers at law firms with current willingness to consider startup products. Fisher reports increased openness across Fortune 1000 enterprises, including large law firms, over the preceding 18–24 months, attributing it to AI-driven change and demand for accurate, contextual solutions. Abramowitz offers his consultancy's shift from outbound sales before November 2022 to inbound business afterward as personal experience, not representative market data.
qs: They've never been more willing to work with early stage startups.
And I think it's because of the pace of change largely driven by AI.
we've seen it for probably the last 18 months, maybe 24 months
pre-November 22, every deal I ever sold was outbound
And since then, every single deal that we have is an inbound.

kp.k: Legal software shifts from records toward performing work
kp.d: Fisher argues that legal technology is moving beyond databases that lawyers consult toward systems that perform actions. He identifies this as a harder engineering, data science and AI challenge, compounded by legal language's contextual dependencies. The opportunity spans both law firms as a vertical market and corporate legal departments across industries.
qs: It's now drastically moving to these systems of action, rather than systems of record.
Not only that, like the words are different, especially in a contract, the words modify each other in a way.
It's also a vertical and a horizontal, like law firms are verticals, but every corporation has a legal department.

kp.k: AI could redirect internal and external professional-services spending
kp.d: Fisher presents an investment thesis, not an established spending outcome: AI could consolidate fragmented expenditure on expensive external advisers and their corporate counterparts. Law firms might use AI to manage business-model changes, while in-house teams might reduce external expenditure and improve efficiency. He therefore sees viable buyers on both sides, potentially sharing systems used in practicing law.
qs: And so our thesis is that AI will drive a lot of these fragmented spend buckets to AI.

And either the external person is going to use it to help smooth over some business model changes and or the corporate in house will use it to reduce some of the spend externally and be more efficient.
it is the act of practicing and that can be in house or it can be external and it's probably going to be shared.

kp.k: AI-native firms might abandon traditional leverage and hourly billing
kp.d: Abramowitz proposes that the ideal legal-AI customer may not yet exist: one or two partners could establish an AI-first firm without the traditional associate leverage model or billable hour. This is the host's hypothetical framing, not evidence of existing restructuring. Levy agrees with the general sense that current products and business arrangements are still immature, explicitly stressing uncertainty while predicting faster change than expected.
qs: Really the best customer for AI today would be like a partner, maybe two partners that want to peel off, start their own firm from scratch
we don't need to use the leverage model anymore. Maybe we don't even use the billable hour model anymore.
This is just a feel in a sense. Like, we don't know.
And I think it's going to get there a little faster than people expect.

kp.k: Complex practices require specialized AI rather than generic substitutes
kp.d: Fisher predicts that repetitive solo or small-firm practices could adopt AI quickly, whereas complex large-firm M&A requires coordination across litigation, IP, real estate and other specialties. He envisages highly contextualized AI companions, associates or partners differentiated by practice area, each potentially supporting a substantial business. Abramowitz extends this into a hypothetical solo M&A partner consulting AI specialists; Fisher qualifies that humans may remain involved.
qs: if you're a solo or small practitioner that does this one thing over and over again, you can probably move to just using that much an AI solution very quickly.
Think about the legal market is actually a bunch of large sub markets by practice area.
it's one that's highly contextualized and specialized by practice area.
And you might still be a human there because you're going to do that.

kp.k: AI assistance still involves human review and fallibility
kp.d: Fisher expects lawyers to retain responsibility for work, comparing future AI supervision with existing partner–associate–paralegal review chains rather than complete substitution. Levy describes using AI to identify contractual risk and double-check his work, while acknowledging that its answers are not always correct. These are expectations and personal usage accounts, not measured accuracy results.
qs: The lawyers I don't think are ever going to let go of the work completely.
They review most of the pieces of work and they trust their senior associate to review the junior associates and the junior review the paralegal.
I check with the AI, which isn't always right.
Everyone wants an AI third year associate.

kp.k: Automating junior work threatens the apprenticeship pipeline
kp.d: Fisher warns that eliminating apprentices would undermine firms' long-term survival. He identifies associate formation as an unmet product opportunity, arguing that a training gap associated with COVID will increase with AI. His example is the loss of learning through listening to partners negotiate and asking questions during muted side conversations; he raises progression from associate to senior associate and then partner as the problem to solve.
qs: the firms are in an apprenticeship model, right? So if you lose all your apprentices, like the firm eventually dies too.
there's a training gap in law. If it started in COVID, it's going to come more with AI.
Like how do you train associates to become senior associates, and how do you train senior associates to become partners?

kp.k: Investors reject a settled two-company legal AI market
kp.d: Asked about Harvey and Legora, Fisher distinguishes their financing and marketing head start from eventual control of legal work. He argues that specialized solutions addressing difficult problems leave substantial room for competitors. Levy similarly describes multiple large legal submarkets with no clear winner. Their bullish views are investment judgments, not demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: they've got a huge head start and they've got a huge war chest
I think this is a market where you're going to have some highly specialized solutions that are hard, solving some of the hardest problems for us.
So I don't think generalization is the way that's going to win this.
So there's room, there's room. And we're early and there aren't great, there isn't a clear winner right now.

kp.k: Hard problems and protected deployment guide investment selection
kp.d: Fisher says Myriad favors companies solving the hardest problem in a specialty before expanding downstream. As a portfolio example, he describes Syntrax using small language models and synthetic data for protected on-premises contract analysis and fine-tuning, and reports an AM5 law firm as its first client. These are an investor's descriptions of portfolio strategy and capabilities, without independent performance evidence in the transcript.
qs: are you solving the hardest problem? Because once you solve that hardest problem, it's easier to move downstream, essentially.
they're using small language models and synthetic data
actually fine tune and keep the information protected, but actually be able to extract really difficult things.
they have an AM5 law firm as their first client

kp.k: Lean AI businesses challenge conventional venture funding assumptions
kp.d: Abramowitz asks whether AI-enabled founders may prefer bootstrapping to venture investment, citing Base 44 as a cross-domain example: he describes a single founder, no employees and $189,000 in profit in the preceding month. Levy says YC debates the question and observes that incoming founders need fewer hires. He predicts job displacement but explicitly rejects confident five-year forecasts and does not establish that bootstrapping will replace venture funding.
qs: has not raised any money, it's entirely bootstrapped. It is a single founder, no employees
And last month, he generated $189,000 in profit.
They don't need to hire as many people. There's going to be job displacement.
I just don't think anybody knows.

kp.k: Founder adaptability matters more than the initial product thesis
kp.d: Levy frames YC's early-stage selection around exceptional technical founders, motivation and their thinking about competitors rather than whether the initial idea appears settled or crowded. Fisher additionally emphasizes fit between founder background and the problem, plus distinctive positioning. Both argue that strong founders can find a viable direction beyond their original pitch; Levy cautions that prior legal expertise can also produce premature dismissal of ideas.
qs: often, it's not about even what they're doing for us because we're so early.
we're looking for folks that have a really talented background, you know, and that has to kind of match the solution they're trying to solve.
you're looking for somebody that has a unique take on the problem, like a unique positioning on it.
It might not be even in the original idea.

kp.k: Unmet opportunities include transaction intelligence and litigation pain
kp.d: Beyond training, Fisher identifies determining what is market for a transaction and managing entities with their governing documents over time as opportunities. Levy favors businesses helping customers make money over compliance products, which he says face difficulty increasing average contract values. He also expresses interest in reducing nuisance-litigation burdens through settlement, funding or risk transfer, but presents this as an undeveloped idea.
qs: the elusive what is market for the transaction you're on.
There should be something that actually manages the entity and the governing docs all the way through like a GL.
I like businesses that help people make money.
It's hard to get average contract values up. Nobody really wants to buy it.
if somebody would come in and just say, I'll fund this or take the risk or something. I don't know. I would have to think about it.

kp.k: Professional services should pursue productization and operational efficiency
kp.d: Responding to an audience question about turning services into products, Abramowitz recommends productization through software, process or revenue-model changes. Fisher argues that professional-services businesses need to examine AI's effects across business operations and professional practice. Levy endorses the urgency. These are strategic recommendations, not evidence that legal services have already become standardized products.
qs: productizing can sometimes be with software, it can sometimes be with process, it can sometimes be with like tweaks to the revenue model.
if you're running, like, a professional services business, you've got to look at how AI and software is going to impact you.
you've got to find ways to run your business and your practice better and more efficient.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Fisher and Levy describe rising startup adoption, a shift toward AI performing legal tasks, opportunities for specialised products, and changes to spending, supervision, training and staffing.
pts.d: Jonathan Levy (06:33–09:04) says legal technology is attracting stronger entrepreneurial talent and that law firms have become more receptive to startup products. Chris Fisher (10:17) attributes unprecedented enterprise willingness to work with early-stage startups largely to AI-driven change. Fisher (14:19) characterises legal software as moving from systems that store information for lawyers to systems of action, creating difficult engineering and contextualisation problems. Fisher (17:01) predicts that AI will capture spending currently divided between expensive internal and external professional services: law firms may use it to adjust their business models, while corporate legal departments may reduce external spending and improve efficiency. Levy (19:19) agrees with the preceding suggestion that existing products and customers are not yet fully aligned, but explicitly calls this a feeling rather than a known outcome and expects improvement faster than people anticipate. Fisher (20:06) predicts quicker adoption for repetitive solo or small-practice work, while complex work will require practice-specific AI companions, associates or partners. He expects lawyers to retain responsibility and use hierarchical review rather than relinquish work completely (21:13). Levy (21:41) describes AI as already useful for checking contract risks, although not consistently correct. Fisher (23:26–24:32) rejects the idea that Harvey and Legora have already settled the market: despite their funding and marketing advantages, he expects specialised solutions addressing hard problems to remain important. Levy (25:04) likewise says there is no clear winner. Fisher (21:13; 30:47) warns that losing apprentices threatens firms' future and that AI will intensify a training gap. In the broader startup and venture-capital domain, Levy (29:00–29:47) predicts reduced hiring needs, job displacement and a different investment model, while declining to predict its precise form. Fisher (38:29), endorsed by Levy, says professional-services businesses must reconsider how AI and software affect their operations and practices.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is predominantly investor and practitioner experience, portfolio examples, customer encounters and personal tool use; the predictions are not supported by formal studies or benchmarks in the transcript.
pts.d: Levy supports his talent and adoption claims with his experience at Y Combinator, comparisons with earlier founders, recollections of law-firm procurement committees, and YC's own product purchasing. His positive assessment of Legora includes a demo and actual use; the auto-caption transcript renders its name inconsistently, including as 'LeCora'. Fisher draws on his legal and corporate-strategy experience, investor conversations, and observations of enterprises and AmLaw firms. He illustrates technical opportunities through portfolio companies addressing IP, chronology, research and contract extraction. In particular, he describes Syntrax using small language models and synthetic data for protected, on-premises contract analysis and reports an 'AM5' firm as its first client; no measured extraction accuracy or efficiency results are supplied. Fisher's spending-reallocation account is explicitly an investment thesis rather than an observed quantified shift. His supervision and apprenticeship arguments rely on analogies to existing law-firm review and training practices. Levy's claim that AI is useful but fallible rests on his own contract-risk checking. His broader displacement prediction draws on what incoming startup founders report about needing fewer hires, without employment counts or a specified dataset. The competitive outlook is informed by portfolio positioning, conference discussions and investor judgement; neither speaker supplies market-share analysis establishing future winners.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The speakers describe an early, rapidly changing market; adoption speed depends on task repetition and practice complexity, and longer-term outcomes remain unspecified.
pts.d: At the conversation published in 2025, Fisher dates increased willingness to work with startups to approximately the preceding 18–24 months. The shift toward systems of action is described as already occurring, while spending redistribution and specialised AI practice roles are forward-looking without a numerical deadline. Levy repeatedly qualifies his outlook as early and uncertain, although he expects progress faster than anticipated. Fisher conditions rapid substitution or heavy reliance on AI on a solo or small practitioner repeatedly doing the same kind of work. Complex AmLaw 200 M&A instead requires multiple areas of expertise and highly contextualised products. Fisher's forecast of continued human involvement qualifies the AI-partner language: it does not mean complete removal of human lawyers or review. Levy's current contract-checking use is explicitly qualified by errors. Fisher acknowledges that Harvey and Legora could still win and possess substantial head starts and funding; his claim is that the wider legal market is not already decided. He ties the training gap to changes beginning during COVID and expects AI to worsen it, without specifying a date. Levy anticipates changes in venture capital over the next few years but expressly rejects confidence about the world five years ahead; his job-displacement claim has no quantified timetable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span law-firm providers, corporate legal buyers, lawyers in training, specialised legal-AI vendors, founders and investors; broader hiring predictions concern startups rather than a measured legal labour-market segment.
pts.d: Fisher identifies both law firms and corporate legal departments as customers for AI systems that perform work. External providers may adapt their business models; in-house departments may retain more work and reduce outside expenditure. Solo and small practices with repetitive workflows may move faster than AmLaw 200 firms handling complex multidisciplinary transactions. M&A, litigation, IP and real-estate practices are examples of distinct specialist needs and potential product markets. Partners, senior associates, junior associates and paralegals appear in Fisher's analogy for human oversight of AI, while associates and senior associates are the groups whose progression and training he identifies as threatened. Legal-AI vendors and their investors face opportunities in multiple large submarkets rather than necessarily a single winner-take-all contest. Fisher's portfolio companies are discussed as software vendors, not as alternative legal service providers delivering outsourced legal work. Levy's broader comments concern startup founders who need fewer employees, potentially displaced workers, and venture investors confronting an uncertain funding model. The discussion does not provide a concrete access-to-justice prediction or evidence of effects on unmet civil legal need.
